title: NATO is looking to create the same battlefield feedback loop Ukraine has
description: In Ukraine, data from the front is relayed to the defense industry, which can quickly field new tech before Russia adapts and it becomes obsolete.
fullText:
NATO wants to establish the same kind of battlefield feedback loop that Ukraine has set up.

In Ukraine, data from the front lines is relayed to industry, which quickly develops new tech.

It is then deployed, often within weeks, before Russia can adapt and render it obsolete.

NATO leadership is looking for ways to mirror Ukraine's battlefield feedback loop, in which issues from the front lines are relayed to the defense industry, which quickly fields solutions for soldiers.

US Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who oversees NATO military operations as the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said Ukraine has built high-level contacts with the defense industry "that allow them to innovate very quickly."

Grynkewich, one of NATO's two strategic commanders, told Business Insider at the Farnborough International Airshow in England this week that some allied countries are already involved in these efforts.

For instance, NATO's Forward Land Forces Battlegroup in Romania, led by France, is buying commercial off-the-shelf technology from trusted vendors and immediately testing it in the field.

"So we've got places where we're learning," Grynkewich said. "That's a whole structural thing that'll take some time to adapt across the entire alliance, but we know where we need to go."

Grynkewich said one of the reasons thay he traveled to Farnborough, which showcases the latest in defense technology, was to build what he described as "connective tissue at the senior level."

Ukrainian officials have likened the arms race between Ukraine and Russia to a cat-and-mouse game. In Kyiv, drones, robots, and other new technologies move from the design phase to field testing and, finally, into the hands of soldiers within weeks or months.

Battlefield feedback is quickly shared with arms makers so that they can develop solutions to pressing issues on the front lines. The goal for Ukraine is to innovate faster than Russia can adapt, especially in new drone capabilities, so the product doesn't become obsolete.

NATO leadership has long praised Ukraine's ability to quickly react to the changing battlefield. Some Western officials have said they want the alliance to demonstrate a similar sense of urgency for weapons development and procurement.

NATO isn't driven by the same wartime pressures as Ukraine, but officials and security experts argue that the alliance can't afford to sit back as it prepares for a potential future confrontation with Russia.

The development cycle for complex systems built by legacy defense contractors for past wars — warships, aircraft, and armored vehicles — can take years. However, newer Western startups breaking into the field are trying to more closely emulate the Ukrainian model.

Some war technologies have a quicker innovation cycle than others.

"All the software-centric capabilities are easy to update," said French Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.

"And so I think we are transitioning from complex-to-update to easy-to-update platforms, intrinsically. That means that the design is now fitted for rapid adaptation," Vandier, NATO's other strategic commander, told Business Insider in an interview this week.

"This is the good news, and I think everybody's going on that. Some are quicker than the others, but it's the global trend," he said.

Because NATO isn't in an active conflict, though, it is hamstrung by regulations and laws that could slow development and innovation.

"I think to match that, we need to have structures that are ready to shift," Vandier said, adding that when the constraints are ultimately lifted, the alliance will be "ready to accelerate."

title: A Ukrainian arms maker says it's got a new high-speed interceptor built to hunt Russia's jet-powered Shaheds
description: Kyiv has said this year that it needs cheap drones to counter Russia's jet-powered drones, the slowest of which already can cruise at 200 mph.
fullText:
A Ukrainian drone maker said it has made an interceptor that can reach top speeds of 230 mph.

That puts SkyFall's P1-Sun JetKiller in comfortable range to take down Russia's jet-powered Shaheds.

Russia has been increasingly using these more advanced loitering munitions to bombard Ukraine.

Ukrainian defense firm SkyFall said on Wednesday that it has developed an interceptor drone capable of taking down Russia's jet-powered Shaheds, a much faster class of attack drone that Moscow is using more regularly.

The P1-SUN JetKiller is designed with a top flight speed of 370 kmph, or 230 mph, at maximum altitudes of 9,000 meters, or roughly 30,000 feet, SkyFall said in a statement.

The drone can remain airborne for 15 minutes with a 500-gram explosive payload and can be configured with cameras for day or night operations, the company added.

Speed and maneuverability are major requirements for an interceptor hoping to catch and destroy a jet-powered Shahed.

Ukrainian interceptor drones were originally built to counter the Geran-1 and Geran-2, Russia's versions of the Iranian propeller-driven Shahed. These fly at top speeds of about 115 mph, but newer models with jet engines, called Geran-3s, can cruise at 200 mph.

Making cheap drones to counter these faster Shaheds has been an uphill task for Ukraine. As Business Insider previously reported, souping up an interceptor drone, which has to be mass-producible and often uses propellers, to reach such speeds requires copious fine-tuning.

The sheer amount of power needed to push quadcopters to 200 mph and above risks overheating the drones, which SkyFall said wouldn't be a problem with the JetKiller in straight-line flight.

SkyFall said the JetKiller is also equipped with an AI-based terminal guidance system, which essentially is a targeting algorithm to guide the drone just as it's about to hit its quarry. Such tech has increasingly been appearing in Ukrainian drones this year.

SkyFall added that the system "allows the interceptor to detect and lock onto enemy targets faster than the human eye at ranges of up to 1 kilometer."

"What's notable is that it's been used already with confirmed intercepts and is reaching mass production," said a company spokesperson, identified only by his call sign, Ares, for security purposes.

Ares told Business Insider that the JetKiller has destroyed over a dozen "jet- powered threats" on the battlefield, and that SkyFall intends to start mass production of these interceptors in August with a monthly target of 50,000 drones.

Kyiv has repeatedly said this year that it's prioritizing low-cost interceptor tech to counter Russia's jet-powered drones. Moscow fields at least three major types of attack drones with jet engines, including the Geran-5, which Ukrainian intelligence warned in January can fly at up to 373 mph.

The JetKiller is now one of the few interceptor drones that Ukrainian manufacturers say can fill the role. The Wild Hornets, another drone maker, told Business Insider's Jake Epstein in May that it's testing a new version of its Sting interceptor designed to destroy jet-powered Shaheds.

title: Kremlin says Russian online retailer Wildberries suffered losses in warehouse attacks
description: MOSCOW, July 21 (Reuters) - Online retailer Wildberries, Russia's answer to Amazon, and the merchants who trade through it are grappling with losses in the wake of Ukrainian attacks on warehouses
fullText:
MOSCOW, July 21 (Reuters) - Online retailer Wildberries, Russia's answer to Amazon, and the merchants who trade through it are grappling with losses in the wake of Ukrainian attacks on warehouses operated by the retailer, the Kremlin said ‌on Tuesday.

Drones targeted two large logistics hubs in the cities of Kotovsk and Elektrostal on Saturday. The strikes killed ‌eight workers, sparked fires and disrupted operations at Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, which can handle over 20 million orders per day.

While the extent of the damage ​remains unclear, the attacks on a company so central to the consumer economy appear to mark a widening of Kyiv's strategy of using long-range drones to disrupt Russia's war effort and pressure the Kremlin to make peace.

Asked about the attacks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists: "The situation is indeed difficult because of the losses suffered both by the company itself and by representatives of small and medium-sized businesses."

He ‌denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military ⁠supplies.

Wildberries started as an online shop reselling apparel from European catalogues. It has since expanded its product range and evolved into a marketplace that includes third-party vendors. Wildberries has not commented on the ⁠scale of the damage.

On Monday, founder Tatyana Kim said the company was aware of many questions about compensation for damaged goods at its Elektrostal facility, but said it needed more time to take stock of the impact of the attacks. She did not say when the ​site ​would reopen.

The Kotovsk facility would resume accepting deliveries on July 23 and ​goods stored there would return to sale, she ‌said in an online post.

Turkish retailer Koton Magazacilik said on Tuesday a portion of its inventory had been affected by damage to the Wildberries sites.

Any protracted disruption to Wildberries' operations is likely to be felt by many across Russia. With over 1 million sellers, the company is one of the main forces behind a rapid nationwide shift to online retail.

Online sales across Russia rose 28% in 2025 to 11.5 trillion roubles ($147 billion), according to the Association of Internet Trade Companies. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said sales of ‌goods and services on digital platforms equate to around 8.5% of GDP.

Ukrainian ​strikes on energy infrastructure have already affected daily life across Russia, prompting the ​authorities to intervene to support the domestic fuel market ​after shortages triggered hours-long lines at gas stations and public unease.

Peskov said the government was in touch ‌with Wildberries in connection with the attacks and was ​helping deal with issues.

On a "We sell ​on WildBerries" group on the Telegram messaging app, some members discussed how to handle sales while the two warehouses were closed.

Others discussed why Ukraine had targeted Wildberries. "Retaliation for their own warehouses," one person wrote, suggesting an explanation for the ​attack, and adding that Ukraine might be trying ‌to inflict "a blow to (Russia's) economy in terms of GDP and jobs".

Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukrainian postal sites and ​energy infrastructure since launching the full-scale invasion in early 2022.

title: Romania says ship heading to Ukraine struck off its coast
description: July 21 (Reuters) - A Liberian-flagged vessel sailing from Egypt to Ukraine has been hit off Romania's coast in an attack likely linked to Russia's war on Ukraine, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said
fullText:
July 21 (Reuters) - A Liberian-flagged vessel sailing from Egypt to Ukraine has been hit ‌off Romania's coast in an attack likely ‌linked to Russia's war on Ukraine, Romanian President Nicusor Dan ​said on Tuesday.

This year, Russian and Ukrainian drones have repeatedly breached the airspace and territorial waters of Romania, officials in the European Union and ‌NATO member state ⁠neighbouring Ukraine have said.

"Last night, the LPG Gas Lisbon, a Liberian-flagged vessel, was ⁠hit outside Romanian territorial waters, approximately 20 nautical miles (40 km) off the Romanian coast," Dan wrote ​on X.

Dan ​said Romanian rescuers had ​evacuated the crew, including ‌three injured members, and a tugboat had been dispatched to ensure the vessel did not drift and pose a danger to navigation.

"State institutions are on alert and will clarify the circumstances, ‌causes and responsibilities related to ​this serious incident, most likely ​part of the ​illegal war of aggression of the ‌Russian Federation against Ukraine," Dan ​said.

Russia, which ​launched a full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has either denied responsibility for reported ​attacks on ‌Romania, said they were carried out by ​Ukraine, or blamed Ukrainian "provocation".
